17.notes: Hint 3 does the elimination for the student instead of asking them to recall the term. Hint 2 already says "Each repeating unit of DNA is itself made of three smaller parts joined together," and the four options are exactly those three parts (Phosphate, Nitrogen base, Deoxyribose sugars) plus the composite (Nucleotides). Hint 3 then says "Look at the four options. Are they all the same size of thing, or is one of them bigger than the others?" - this converts the answer into a mechanical odd-one-out spotting task (three options are parts, one is the whole), so a student can pick C without recalling or understanding what a nucleotide actually is. That fails the hint 3 test: reading it, the student answers without thinking about the biology.
17.fix: Hint 3: You already know each repeating unit has three parts joined together. Which single word names that whole joined unit, rather than one of the three parts on its own?

22.notes: Hint 3 reduces the choice to a grammar-matching trick rather than biology recall. After hint 2 narrows to Apical and Meristematic, hint 3 says: "Of the two options left, one word tells you where the cells are and the other tells you what kind of cells they are. Which does the question ask for?" The question stem itself says "What type of cells," so a student only has to match the word "type" in the stem to "what kind of cells they are" in the hint, without needing to know anything about meristems. That lets the student answer without thinking, failing the hint 3 test.
22.fix: Hint 3: The question asks what type of cells these are, not where in the plant they sit. Recall the name for small, thin-walled cells that keep dividing, whichever meristem they are part of.

29.notes: Hint 3 resolves the question by pure elimination before its own closing question does any work: "Of the three options left, two involve the cell doing physical work, pulling fibres or parts of the cell. Ask which one could happen even across a non-living membrane." A student only needs to match "pulling fibres" to muscle contraction and "parts of the cell" being pulled to mitosis (chromosomes) to identify both of those two immediately; the remaining option, osmosis, is then the answer by elimination, without the student ever needing to reason about the non-living membrane fact the hint poses as its question. This fails the hint 3 test: the student can answer without thinking, from the grouping clue alone.
29.fix:
Hint 2: Active transport moves substances against a concentration gradient, and mitosis needs the cell to pull its own chromosomes apart, so both use ATP.
Hint 3: Of the two options left, one needs the cell's muscle fibres to slide past each other, using energy. Could the other one happen just as well through a dead, non-living membrane?

31.notes: Hint 3 is answerable by logic alone, without any eye anatomy knowledge: "Of the two options left, one is a fixed, clear layer and the other can change. Which could control the amount of light?" Controlling an amount requires the ability to vary, and the hint has already told the student that only one of the two remaining options "can change"; the student needs no fact about the iris or cornea to pick it. This fails the hint 3 test that a student should not be able to answer without thinking.
31.fix: Hint 3: Of the two options left, one is a clear, curved layer that light passes through first and does not contain muscle. The other is a ring of muscle around the pupil. Which one is the ring of muscle?

38.notes: Hint 2 says: "Every living cell releases energy from food, and every living thing gets bigger and responds to its surroundings in some way." This restates all three wrong options almost word for word ("releases energy from food" = respiration = B, "gets bigger" = growth = C, "responds to its surroundings" = irritability = D), leaving Locomotion as the only option not described, so the answer is stated indirectly after only two hints. Hint 3 then says: "Ask which feature a rooted plant does not show: does a mango tree move its whole body from one place to another?" This is the dictionary definition of locomotion (option A), so a student can match it to the option by vocabulary alone, with no biological reasoning left to do. This fails hint 2's rule against stating the answer indirectly and hint 3's test that a student must not be able to answer without thinking.
38.fix:
Hint 2: Every living cell respires to release energy, and every living thing grows during its life, whether or not it is able to move about.
Hint 3: A mango tree still responds to touch, light and gravity even though it stays rooted in one place. Of the two features left, which one means reacting to a stimulus, and which one means moving the whole organism to a new place?
